papers.title: Nouns: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on nouns, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The school has ordered some new ____ for the staff room.
questions.explanation:
*Furniture* is an uncountable noun: it never takes -s and never follows *a*. *Some new furniture* is correct.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- furnitures: *Furniture* is uncountable, so it has no plural form with -s.
- furniture's: The apostrophe shows possession, not a plural. Nothing here belongs to the furniture.
- a furniture: Uncountable nouns do not take *a* or *an*. Say *a piece of furniture*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Two ____ stopped to help the motorcyclist who had fallen at the roundabout.
questions.explanation:
In compounds such as *passer-by*, *mother-in-law* and *commander-in-chief*, the main noun takes the plural: *passers-by*, *mothers-in-law*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- passer-bys: In a compound noun like this, the main word (*passer*) takes the plural ending, not *by*.
- passers-bys: Only one part of the compound takes the plural ending: *passers-by*.
- passer-by's: The apostrophe makes it possessive, not plural.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The ____ playground was flooded after the heavy rain, so the pupils stayed indoors.
questions.explanation:
Plurals that do not end in -s (*children, men, women, people*) form the possessive with *'s*: *the children's playground*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- childrens': *Children* is already plural, so the possessive is *children's*, not *childrens'*.
- childrens: There is no word *childrens*: *children* is the plural of *child*.
- children: Without the apostrophe and *s*, the noun does not show that the playground belongs to the children.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The career counsellor gave us some useful ____ about choosing our WASSCE subjects.
questions.explanation:
*Advice* (noun, with a *c*) is uncountable. *Advise* (with an *s*) is the verb: *She advised us to study*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- advices: *Advice* is uncountable, so it has no plural with -s. Say *pieces of advice*.
- an advice: Uncountable nouns do not take *a* or *an*.
- advise: *Advise* is the verb (to advise someone). After *some useful* we need the noun, *advice*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The ____ of the two neighbouring villages met at the chiefdom headquarters to settle the land dispute.
questions.explanation:
Some nouns ending in -f change to -ves (*leaf, leaves*; *knife, knives*), but *chief*, *roof*, *belief* and *proof* just add -s: *chiefs*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chieves: *Chief* is one of the -f nouns that simply add -s, like *roofs* and *beliefs*.
- chiefes: There is no *-es* ending here: the plural is *chiefs*.
- chief's: The apostrophe shows possession, not a plural.

papers.title: Pronouns: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on pronouns, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Between you and ____, I do not think the bus will leave on time today.
questions.explanation:
A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form: *between you and me*, *for him and her*, *with us*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- I: After a preposition (*between*) we need the object form, *me*, not the subject form *I*.
- myself: *Myself* is reflexive: it is used when the subject is also *I*, as in *I hurt myself*.
- mine: *Mine* is a possessive pronoun (*the book is mine*). It cannot follow *between you and*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The girl ____ father owns the shop at Lumley is my classmate.
questions.explanation:
*Whose* shows possession in a relative clause: *the girl whose father owns the shop* = the girl's father owns the shop.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- who's: *Who's* means *who is* or *who has*. *Who is father owns* makes no sense.
- whom: *Whom* is an object pronoun. Here we need possession: the father belongs to the girl.
- which: *Which* refers to things, not people, and does not show possession.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Fatmata cut ____ while slicing onions for the family's dinner.
questions.explanation:
When the subject and the object are the same person, use a reflexive pronoun: *Fatmata cut herself*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- herselves: *-selves* is the plural ending (*themselves*). One person takes *herself*.
- hisself: *Hisself* is not standard English, and Fatmata needs a feminine pronoun.
- her own: *Her own* must be followed by a noun, for example *her own finger*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

This calculator is not yours; it is ____.
questions.explanation:
A possessive pronoun stands alone in place of a noun, with no apostrophe: *it is hers* (= her calculator).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- her's: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: *hers, his, its, ours, yours, theirs*.
- her: *Her* needs a noun after it (*her calculator*). On its own we need *hers*.
- hers': Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The poda-poda ____ broke down on the bridge has been towed away.
questions.explanation:
For things, the relative pronoun is *which* (or *that*): *the poda-poda which broke down*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- who: *Who* refers to people. A poda-poda is a thing.
- whom: *Whom* refers to people, and only as an object.
- whose: *Whose* shows possession. Here the vehicle is the subject of *broke down*.

papers.title: Verbs and Verb Forms: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on verbs and verb forms, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

By the time we reached the gate, the bell had already ____.
questions.explanation:
*Ring* is irregular: *ring, rang, rung*. The past perfect is *had* + past participle: *had rung*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rang: *Rang* is the simple past. After *had* we need the past participle, *rung*.
- ringed: *Ringed* is the past of a different verb, *to ring* meaning to circle something, as in *ringed in red*.
- ring: After *had* we need the past participle, not the base form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Every morning the sun ____ in the east.
questions.explanation:
*Rise* (rise, rose, risen) has no object; *raise* (raise, raised, raised) always has one. A habit or fact takes the present simple: *the sun rises*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- raises: *Raise* needs an object: you raise your hand. The sun does not raise anything.
- rise: With a singular subject (*the sun*) the present simple takes -s: *rises*.
- arouses: *Arouse* means to stir up a feeling, as in *arouse interest*. It does not describe the sun coming up.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

After the long journey from Kabala, my grandfather went to ____ down for an hour.
questions.explanation:
*Lie* (to rest flat) has no object: *lie, lay, lain*. *Lay* (to put down) has an object: *lay, laid, laid*. After *to*, use the base form: *to lie down*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lay: *Lay* needs an object: you lay a mat or lay a table. Here nothing is being laid.
- laid: *Laid* is the past of *lay*. After *to* we need the base form.
- lain: *Lain* is the past participle of *lie*. After *to* we need the base form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The football match was ____ because the field was flooded.
questions.explanation:
*Call off* means to cancel: *the match was called off because the field was flooded*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- called up: *Call up* means to telephone someone or to summon them, for example for national service.
- called on: *Call on* means to visit someone or to ask someone to speak.
- called out: *Call out* means to shout or to summon help, as in *call out the fire service*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

My father made me ____ my homework before supper.
questions.explanation:
*Make*, *let* and *have* take the base form without *to*: *made me do*, *let us go*. (In the passive it is *I was made to do*.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- to do: After *make* + object in the active voice, we use the base form without *to*.
- doing: *Make* is not followed by an -ing form in this pattern.
- did: The verb after *made me* stays in the base form; the tense is already shown by *made*.

papers.title: Tenses: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on tenses, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Kadiatu ____ in Bo since 2019.
questions.explanation:
An action that started in the past and continues now, with *since* or *for*, takes the present perfect: *has lived* (or *has been living*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lives: *Since 2019* links the past to now, which needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
- lived: The simple past describes finished time. *Since 2019* means she still lives there.
- is living: The present continuous does not combine with *since* + a point in time.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

By the time we got to the bus park, the last bus to Makeni ____.
questions.explanation:
For the earlier of two past actions, especially with *by the time*, use the past perfect: *had left*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has left: The story is in the past (*got*), so the earlier action needs the past perfect, *had left*.
- left: *By the time* + past shows that the leaving happened earlier, which needs the past perfect.
- leaves: The present simple does not fit a story told in the past.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

I will call you as soon as I ____ home.
questions.explanation:
In time clauses about the future (*as soon as, when, before, after, until*), use the present simple: *as soon as I get home*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- will get: After *as soon as*, *when*, *before* and *until*, English uses the present simple for the future, not *will*.
- got: The call is in the future, so the past tense does not fit.
- am getting: The present continuous does not fit a single future moment after *as soon as*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Look! The children ____ in the rain.
questions.explanation:
An action in progress at the moment of speaking takes the present continuous: *are playing*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- play: *Look!* shows the action is happening now, which needs the present continuous.
- have played: The present perfect describes a finished action with a result, not something we can watch now.
- played: The simple past describes finished time, but *Look!* means right now.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

While I was reading for my exams, the light suddenly ____ off.
questions.explanation:
A long action in progress takes the past continuous (*was reading*); the short action that interrupts it takes the simple past (*went off*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- goes: The sentence is in the past (*was reading*), so the sudden action needs the simple past.
- has gone: The present perfect does not fit a story set in the past.
- had went: *Went* is the simple past; after *had* the participle is *gone*. And the past perfect is not needed here.

papers.title: Active and Passive Voice: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on active and passive voice, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The new classroom block ____ by the Minister of Education next Friday.
questions.explanation:
The future passive is *will be* + past participle: *will be opened by the Minister*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- will open: *By the Minister* shows that someone else does the opening, so the verb must be passive.
- will opened: After *will* we need *be* + past participle in the passive: *will be opened*.
- is opening: The block does not open itself, and *by the Minister* calls for the passive.

questions.stem:
Which option is the correct passive form of this sentence?

*The teacher marked the scripts.*
questions.explanation:
To make the passive, the object (*the scripts*) becomes the subject, the verb becomes *be* in the same tense + past participle (*were marked*), and the doer follows *by*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The scripts was marked by the teacher.  
  *Scripts* is plural, so the verb is *were*, not *was*.
- The scripts are marked by the teacher.  
  The active sentence is in the past (*marked*), so the passive must be past too.
- The teacher was marked by the scripts.  
  The teacher did the marking, so the teacher stays as the doer (*by the teacher*).

options.label: A
options.content: The scripts was marked by the teacher.

options.label: B
options.content: The scripts were marked by the teacher.

options.label: C
options.content: The scripts are marked by the teacher.

options.label: D
options.content: The teacher was marked by the scripts.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

English ____ in many West African countries.
questions.explanation:
The present simple passive is *am/is/are* + past participle: *English is spoken*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is speaking: A language does not speak; people speak it. That needs the passive.
- speaks: Active *speaks* would mean English itself does the speaking.
- is spoke: The passive uses the past participle, *spoken*, not the past tense *spoke*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The thief ____ before he could escape with the money.
questions.explanation:
The thief receives the action, so the verb is passive: *was* + past participle *caught*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- was catched: *Catch* is irregular: *catch, caught, caught*. There is no *catched*.
- caught: Active *caught* needs an object (caught someone). Here the thief is the one caught.
- had catch: This is neither a correct past perfect (*had caught*) nor a passive.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

All answers must ____ in blue or black ink.
questions.explanation:
The passive after a modal is modal + *be* + past participle: *must be written*, *can be done*, *should be answered*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- written: After a modal (*must*) the passive needs *be*: *must be written*.
- be wrote: The passive uses the past participle *written*, not the past tense *wrote*.
- being written: After a modal we need the base form *be*, not *being*.

papers.title: Non-finite Verb Forms: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on non-finite verb forms, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

We are looking forward to ____ our WASSCE results.
questions.explanation:
*Look forward to*, *object to* and *be used to* end in the preposition *to*, which takes a gerund: *looking forward to receiving*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- receive: In *look forward to*, *to* is a preposition, so it is followed by an -ing form, not the base form.
- received: A preposition is followed by an -ing form (a gerund), not a past form.
- be receiving: After the preposition *to* we need the gerund *receiving* on its own.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

After his father's illness, Sorie decided ____ a doctor.
questions.explanation:
*Decide*, *hope*, *plan*, *agree* and *refuse* take the to-infinitive: *decided to become*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- becoming: *Decide* is followed by the to-infinitive, not the -ing form.
- become: *Decide* needs *to* before the verb.
- becomes: After *decided* the second verb is non-finite (*to become*); it does not change for the subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly written?
questions.explanation:
A participle phrase at the start of a sentence must describe the subject that follows it. *Walking to school, I saw…* is correct because *I* was walking.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Walking to school, a snake was seen on the path.  
  This says the snake was walking to school: the participle has no correct subject (a dangling participle).
- Walked to school, I saw a snake on the path.  
  The participle for an action in progress is *walking*, not *walked*.
- To walking to school, I saw a snake on the path.  
  *To* does not go with an -ing form here.

options.label: A
options.content: Walking to school, a snake was seen on the path.

options.label: B
options.content: Walked to school, I saw a snake on the path.

options.label: C
options.content: To walking to school, I saw a snake on the path.

options.label: D
options.content: Walking to school, I saw a snake on the path.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The suspect avoided ____ the question about where he was that night.
questions.explanation:
*Avoid*, *enjoy*, *finish*, *deny* and *mind* take the gerund: *avoided answering*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- to answer: *Avoid* is followed by the -ing form, not the to-infinitive.
- answer: *Avoid* needs a gerund after it.
- answered: The second verb is non-finite: *avoided answering*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

____ his homework, Amadu went out to play football.
questions.explanation:
*Having* + past participle shows that one action was complete before the next: *Having finished his homework, Amadu went out*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Have finished: A perfect participle phrase starts with *having*, not *have*.
- Had finished: *Had finished* needs a subject (*He had finished*); it cannot open the sentence like this.
- Being finished: *Being finished* would mean Amadu himself was finished. The homework was finished first.

papers.title: Adjectives: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on adjectives, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Of the two sisters, Isatu is the ____.
questions.explanation:
When comparing exactly two, use the comparative: *the taller of the two*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- tallest: The superlative compares three or more. With *of the two*, use the comparative.
- more taller: Do not use *more* with an -er comparative: that doubles the comparison.
- most tall: *Tall* forms its comparison with -er/-est, and two people take the comparative.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

She wore a ____ dress to her sister's wedding.
questions.explanation:
Adjectives usually follow this order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, then the noun: *a beautiful long red cotton dress*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- red long beautiful cotton: Opinion adjectives (*beautiful*) come before size (*long*) and colour (*red*).
- cotton beautiful long red: The material (*cotton*) comes last, just before the noun.
- long beautiful cotton red: Opinion comes before size, and colour comes before material.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The students were ____ by the long lecture on a hot afternoon.
questions.explanation:
-ed adjectives describe how someone feels (*bored, interested, tired*); -ing adjectives describe what causes it (*boring, interesting, tiring*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- boring: *Boring* describes the thing that causes the feeling (*the lecture was boring*), not how the students felt.
- bore: *Bore* is a noun or a verb, not the adjective we need after *were*.
- boredom: *Boredom* is a noun. After *were* we need an adjective.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

This year's rice harvest is ____ than last year's because the rains came late.
questions.explanation:
*Bad* compares irregularly: *bad, worse, worst*. With *than* use the comparative: *worse than*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- worst: *Worst* is the superlative. With *than* we need the comparative.
- more worse: *Worse* is already comparative; *more* doubles it.
- badder: *Bad* is irregular: *bad, worse, worst*. There is no *badder*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

There is very ____ water left in the tank, so we must fetch more from the well.
questions.explanation:
*Little* goes with uncountable nouns (*little water, little time*); *few* goes with countable plurals. *Very little* means almost none.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- few: *Few* is used with countable plural nouns (*few buckets*). *Water* is uncountable.
- many: *Many* goes with countable plural nouns, and *very many* would mean a lot.
- a few: *A few* is for countable nouns, and it means *some*, which does not fit *we must fetch more*.

papers.title: Prepositions: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on prepositions, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The English paper will begin ____ 9 a.m.
questions.explanation:
Use *at* for clock times (*at 9 a.m.*), *on* for days and dates, and *in* for months, years and parts of the day.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- on: *On* is used with days and dates (*on Monday, on 5 May*), not clock times.
- in: *In* is used with months, years and parts of the day (*in May, in the morning*).
- for: *For* shows how long something lasts, not when it starts.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The young man was accused ____ stealing a goat from the market.
questions.explanation:
Some verbs always take the same preposition: *accuse someone of*, *charge someone with*, *blame someone for*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- for: *Accuse* is followed by *of*, not *for*. (We say *blamed for* or *arrested for*.)
- with: *Charged with* is correct, but *accused* takes *of*.
- about: *Accuse* does not take *about*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Aminata is very good ____ Mathematics.
questions.explanation:
*Good at*, *bad at* and *clever at* describe skill in something: *good at Mathematics*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in: In standard English, *good* takes *at* for a skill or subject: *good at Mathematics*.
- on: *Good on* is not used for skill in a subject.
- with: *Good with* is used for handling people or things (*good with children*), not for a subject.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

We have been waiting for the ferry ____ two hours.
questions.explanation:
With the present perfect continuous, use *for* + a length of time (*for two hours*) and *since* + a starting point (*since 8 o'clock*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- since: *Since* goes with a starting point (*since 8 o'clock*), not a length of time.
- from: *From* needs an end point (*from 8 to 10 o'clock*), and does not show a length of time on its own.
- during: *During* tells us when something happens, not how long it has lasted.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mohamed is married ____ a nurse who works at Connaught Hospital.
questions.explanation:
*Be married to someone* is the standard pattern, like *engaged to* and *related to*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- with: In standard English the phrase is *married to*, not *married with*.
- by: *Married by* would mean the person who performed the wedding.
- for: *Married for* is followed by a length of time (*married for ten years*), not a person.

papers.title: Conjunctions: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on conjunctions, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

____ it was raining heavily, the inter-secondary sports went on.
questions.explanation:
*Although* (or *though*, *even though*) joins two contrasting clauses: *Although it was raining, the sports went on*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Because: *Because* gives a reason. The rain is not the reason the sports went on; it is a contrast.
- Despite: *Despite* is followed by a noun or -ing form (*despite the rain*), not a full clause.
- Unless: *Unless* means *if not*, which does not fit two facts that both happened.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

You will fail the examination ____ you study harder.
questions.explanation:
*Unless* means *if… not*: *You will fail unless you study harder* = *If you do not study harder, you will fail*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- if: *If you study harder, you will fail* says the opposite of what is meant.
- although: *Although* shows contrast; the sentence needs a condition.
- because: *Because* gives a reason; studying harder is not the reason for failing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Neither the teacher ____ the pupils knew where the key was.
questions.explanation:
Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs: *neither… nor*, *either… or*, *both… and*, *not only… but also*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- or: *Neither* pairs with *nor*; *either* pairs with *or*.
- and: *Neither… and* is not a correct pair.
- but: *Neither… but* is not a correct pair.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Not only did Hawa pass all her subjects, ____ she also won a scholarship.
questions.explanation:
*Not only… but also* adds a second, stronger point: *Not only did she pass, but she also won a scholarship*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- and: *Not only* pairs with *but (also)*, not *and*.
- so: *So* shows a result; the sentence adds a second achievement.
- yet: *Yet* shows contrast, but the pair here is *not only… but also*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

He ran all the way to the junction ____ he would not miss the last bus.
questions.explanation:
*So that* introduces a clause of purpose: *He ran so that he would not miss the bus*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- such that: *Such that* describes a result or a degree (*the noise was such that…*), not a purpose.
- in order to: *In order to* is followed by a base verb (*in order not to miss*), not a full clause with *he would*.
- so as: *So as* is followed by *to* + verb (*so as not to miss*), not a clause.

papers.title: Subject-Verb Agreement: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on subject-verb agreement, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Mathematics ____ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation:
Names of subjects ending in -s, such as *Mathematics*, *Economics* and *Physics*, take a singular verb: *Mathematics is*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are: Subjects that end in -s (*Mathematics, Physics, Economics*) are singular nouns.
- were: This is plural and past; the subject is singular and the sentence is about now.
- have been: *Have* is plural; a singular subject takes *has been*, and the simple *is* fits best.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Each of the candidates ____ given a seat number before the examination.
questions.explanation:
*Each*, *every*, *either* and *neither* are singular: *Each of the candidates was given…*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- were: The subject is *each*, which is singular, even though *candidates* comes just before the verb.
- are: *Each* is singular and the sentence is in the past.
- have been: *Each* is singular, so it would take *has been*, not *have been*.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The principal, together with his staff, ____ the visitors at the gate every year.
questions.explanation:
Phrases such as *together with*, *as well as* and *along with* do not change the number of the subject: *The principal, together with his staff, welcomes…*

**Why the other options are wrong**

- welcome: The subject is *the principal* (singular). *Together with his staff* does not make it plural.
- are welcoming: *Are* is plural, and *every year* calls for the present simple.
- have welcomed: *Have* is plural, and the subject *the principal* is singular.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

Neither the boys nor their sister ____ coming to the party.
questions.explanation:
With *neither… nor* and *either… or*, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it: *…nor their sister is*.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- are: With *neither… nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, *their sister*, which is singular.
- were: The nearer subject is singular, and the sentence is in the present.
- have: *Have* is plural and does not form *coming* correctly here.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence.

The number of students who passed English ____ increased this year.
questions.explanation:
*The number of…* is singular (*the number has increased*); *a number of…* means *several* and is plural (*a number of students have passed*).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- have: The subject is *the number*, which is singular. (*A number of students have…* is plural.)
- were: *Were* is plural and past, and it does not form a tense with *increased*.
- are: *Are increased* is not the right tense, and *the number* is singular.
